title: LLMOps
scopeHtml: Scope: Observability, versioning, evals in CI, rollouts, feedback loops and drift.

notes.title: Observability
notes.html:
What to capture per request (trace).

  • Identifiers: trace id, user/tenant, session, feature, environment.
  • Versions: prompt version, model + snapshot id, parameters (temperature, max tokens), tool/schema versions, retrieval config, embedding model, guardrail policy version.
  • Inputs/outputs (with redaction): user message, rewritten query, retrieved chunk ids + scores, final prompt size, response, citations.
  • Execution: each model call and tool call as spans with latency, tokens (input/output/cached), cost, status, retries, finish reason.
  • Outcomes: user feedback, thumbs, edits, escalation, downstream success events.
  • Safety events: guardrail triggers, refusals, flagged content.

Metrics and dashboards.

  • Latency: TTFT, total, p50/p95/p99 per stage.
  • Throughput and queue depth; error rates by type (4xx, 429, 5xx, timeouts, validation failures).
  • Tokens and cost by feature/tenant/model; cache hit rates.
  • Quality proxies: groundedness/judge scores on sampled traffic, thumbs-up rate, escalation rate, retry/regeneration rate.
  • Safety: refusal rate, guardrail triggers, flagged outputs.
  • Retrieval: empty-result rate, average top score, recall probes.

Tooling. OpenTelemetry (GenAI semantic conventions), Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Datadog/Grafana plus custom evaluators, provider consoles.

Privacy. Redact PII/secrets in traces, restrict access, set retention, support deletion; sample full prompts rather than storing everything when sensitive.

Alerting. SLO-based alerts (latency, error rate), cost anomaly alerts, quality drop alerts (judge score or thumbs-down spike), safety incident alerts.

Real life. The instrument panel and flight recorder of an airplane.

notes.title: Versioning everything
notes.html:
Versioned artifacts. Prompts and templates; model identifiers (pin dated snapshots, not floating aliases); sampling parameters; tool definitions and schemas; retrieval configuration (chunking, embedding model, index version, reranker); guardrail policies; evaluation datasets and graders; fine-tuned weights/adapters; application code.

Why. Any layer can change behaviour. Without versions you can't explain a regression, reproduce an answer, roll back precisely, or satisfy audits.

How.

  • Git for prompts/configs; or a prompt registry with immutable versions, labels (prod, staging), and change logs.
  • Attach a manifest (all versions) to each deployment and to each trace.
  • Immutable index versions with aliases; blue/green re-indexing.
  • Semantic versioning for schemas with backward-compatibility rules.
  • Dependency tracking (a schema change needs coordinated prompt, parser, consumer updates).
  • Reproducibility: record seeds where supported, but remember outputs may still vary.

Real life. Batch numbers on food products allow targeted recalls.

notes.title: Evals in CI/CD
notes.html:
Pipeline.

  1. Pre-commit/PR: fast checks: prompt lint, schema validation, unit tests for parsers/tools, small smoke eval (20 to 50 cases, cached where inputs unchanged).
  2. PR eval: golden set run for changes touching prompts/retrieval/models/tools; compare to baseline with confidence intervals; fail on regression beyond thresholds; post a report (score deltas by slice, new failures with examples).
  3. Nightly/weekly: full eval, adversarial/red-team suite, long-tail slices, cost/latency benchmarks, judge calibration drift check.
  4. Pre-release: shadow/canary stage with live metrics.
  5. Post-release: monitor online metrics and sampled auto-eval; feed failures into the dataset.

Practicalities. Control cost with sampling and caching of unchanged cases; pin the judge model; handle non-determinism with repeats; separate flaky tests; store results over time to chart trends; require human sign-off for safety-critical changes.

Real life. The assembly line's quality gate before shipping.

notes.title: Rollouts and experiments
notes.html:
Release strategies.

  • Feature flags for prompts/models/tools, per tenant or percentage.
  • Shadow: run new version in parallel, don't show output; compare.
  • Canary: 1 to 5% of traffic, auto-rollback on SLO/guardrail breaches.
  • A/B tests: randomize users, predefine primary metric and guardrails, adequate sample size and duration, analyze by segment.
  • Interleaving for ranking tasks.
  • Progressive delivery and kill switches.

Guardrail metrics. Latency, error rate, cost per request, safety violations, refusal rate, escalation rate, complaint rate.

Model upgrades. Treat as a release: eval on your suite, review diffs on failures, adjust prompts, shadow test, canary, keep rollback to the previous snapshot until stable.

Real life. Trying a new recipe at one branch before the whole chain.

notes.title: Feedback loops and data flywheel
notes.html:
Signals.

  • Explicit: thumbs up/down with reason, ratings, comments, "report" button, human corrections.
  • Implicit: regenerate, copy/paste, edits to the output, abandonment, follow-up reformulations, escalations to human, task completion events.
  • Expert review: sampled transcripts labelled by domain experts.
  • Automated evaluation on sampled traffic (judges, validators).

Loop. Collect → triage and cluster failures → root-cause (retrieval, prompt, tool, model, data) → fix → add as regression cases → evaluate → release → measure. Periodically use curated corrections as fine-tuning or few-shot data (with consent, privacy review and deduplication).

Pitfalls. Feedback bias (only extremes respond), feedback gaming, privacy/consent for reuse of user data, feedback loops reinforcing the model's own outputs (training on its output), noisy labels.

Real life. A restaurant reading comment cards every week and adjusting the menu.

notes.title: Drift and maintenance
notes.html:
Sources of drift.

  • Model drift: provider updates, deprecations, behaviour changes in unpinned aliases.
  • Data drift: new topics, products, languages in user queries; changing document corpus.
  • Concept drift: policies and definitions change (new refund policy).
  • Infrastructure drift: library upgrades, tokenizer or API changes.
  • Adversary drift: new jailbreak techniques.
  • Embedding/index drift: stale or mixed vectors.

Controls. Pin versions; scheduled eval runs on production samples; monitor distribution of queries (topic clustering, embedding drift), retrieval hit rates and judge scores over time; alert on shifts; periodic re-index and prompt review; deprecation calendar with migration drills; maintain an abstraction layer; regular red-team refresh.

Real life. Servicing a car on schedule, not only when it breaks.

notes.title: Reliability patterns
notes.html:
Failure types. Provider outage, rate limits (429), overload (5xx/529), timeouts, slow responses, malformed outputs, tool failures, retrieval failures, partial stream drops, quota exhaustion.

Patterns.

  • Timeouts on every external call, with budget propagation (deadline).
  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors; honor retry-after; limit attempts; don't retry bad requests; avoid retry storms (retry budget, only one layer retries).
  • Circuit breakers to stop hammering failing dependencies.
  • Fallbacks: secondary model/provider, cached or simplified answer, non-AI path, queue for later.
  • Graceful degradation: disable optional features (reranking, long memory) under load; shed low-priority traffic.
  • Bulkheads: isolate pools per feature/tenant.
  • Idempotency for retried requests with side effects.
  • Health checks and load balancing; multi-region where required.
  • Chaos/fire drills: test failover regularly.
  • SLOs and error budgets to balance reliability with change velocity.

Real life. A backup generator and manual override for when the grid fails.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Observability. Trace each request with all versions, prompts/outputs (redacted), retrieval ids/scores, model/tool spans, tokens, latency, cost, feedback and safety events; dashboards for latency percentiles, errors, cost, cache hits, quality proxies, retrieval health; SLO and anomaly alerts; privacy controls.

Versioning. Pin model snapshots; version prompts, tools, schemas, retrieval/index configs, guardrail policies and datasets; manifest per deployment and trace; immutable versions and aliases; precise rollback and audit.

CI/CD evals. Smoke on PR, golden set with thresholds on config changes, nightly full/adversarial suites, pre-release shadow/canary, post-release monitoring; control cost via sampling/caching; handle non-determinism.

Rollouts. Flags, shadow, canary, A/B with guardrail metrics, kill switches; model upgrades as full releases.

Feedback flywheel. Explicit + implicit + expert signals → triage → fix → regression cases → release; mind bias, consent and self-training loops.

Drift. Model, data, concept, infrastructure, adversary and embedding drift; pin, monitor, schedule re-evaluation and migrations.

Reliability. Timeouts, backoff with jitter and retry-after, single retry layer, circuit breakers, fallbacks, degradation, bulkheads, idempotency, drills, SLOs.

Interview one-liners.

  • "If you can't say which prompt and model version produced an answer, you can't operate the system."
  • "Pin model snapshots; upgrade like a release."
  • "Retries belong in one layer, with jitter and budgets."
  • "Production failures are the best eval cases you will ever get."

questions.subtopic: What to trace per LLM request
questions.promptHtml: What is LLMOps, and what would you record for every LLM request in production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you see an LLM app as a system you must operate, not a prompt you ship once.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: LLMOps is the operational discipline around LLM apps: tracing, versioning, evals, rollouts and monitoring. Because model output is non-deterministic, you cannot debug by re-running. So for every request I record a trace: ids (trace, user, feature), all versions (prompt, model snapshot, parameters, tools, retrieval config), redacted input and output, retrieved chunk ids and scores, each model and tool call as a span with latency, tokens, cost and finish reason, and outcomes like thumbs or escalation. It is the flight recorder of the system.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Plain words first: a trace is the full record of one request; a span is one step inside it (one model call, one tool call, one retrieval). TTFT is time to first token, the delay before the user sees any text.

request -> [retrieve span] -> [LLM span] -> [tool span] -> [LLM span] -> response
              ids+scores       tokens,cost     args,result    finish_reason
every span carries: prompt_version, model_snapshot, params, latency, status

Why the versions matter: when quality drops you must answer "which prompt, which model, which index produced this?" Without that, a regression is unexplainable. Next, metrics derived from traces: latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) per stage, error rate by type (429, 5xx, timeout, schema failure), tokens and cost per feature/tenant, cache hit rate, quality proxies (sampled judge score, thumbs-up rate, regeneration rate), retrieval health (empty-result rate, top score), safety (refusal and guardrail rates). Tools: OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Datadog/Grafana.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import time, uuid
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()  # key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

def traced_call(prompt_version, user_msg):
    t0 = time.time()
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=300,
                               messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_msg}])
    span = {"trace_id": str(uuid.uuid4()), "prompt_version": prompt_version,
            "model": r.model, "in_tok": r.usage.input_tokens, "out_tok": r.usage.output_tokens,
            "stop": r.stop_reason, "latency_ms": int((time.time() - t0) * 1000)}
    print(span)  # ship to your trace backend instead; redact user_msg before storing
    return r
// Kotlin: wrap whatever client you use (Anthropic Java SDK or your backend); the span shape is the point
data class Span(val traceId: String, val promptVersion: String, val model: String,
                val inTok: Long, val outTok: Long, val stop: String, val latencyMs: Long)

inline fun <T> timed(block: () -> T): Pair<T, Long> {
    val t0 = System.nanoTime(); val r = block()
    return r to (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000
}
// Java: same span record; fill it from the SDK response usage fields (verify exact getters in the SDK docs)
record Span(String traceId, String promptVersion, String model,
            long inTok, long outTok, String stop, long latencyMs) {}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Logging only the final answer, not the retrieved context and versions.
  • Storing raw prompts with PII and no retention policy.
  • Watching only average latency; the tail (p99) is what users complain about.
  • No cost attribution per tenant or feature.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is re-running a bad request not enough? → Sampling is random and context (retrieval, tools) may have changed; the trace is the only faithful record.
  2. Which alerts? → SLO latency/error, cost anomaly, quality (judge/thumbs) drop, safety triggers.
  3. How do you avoid trace storage blowing up? → Sample full payloads, always keep metadata, set retention.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "log prompts and responses." Senior: versions manifest on every span, redaction, cost and quality metrics per slice, alerts tied to SLOs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team could not explain a complaint spike because traces lacked the prompt version; a day was lost bisecting deploys.

questions.promptHtml: Why should you pin a dated model snapshot instead of using a floating alias like "latest"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests awareness that the model is a dependency that can change under you.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A floating alias silently points to a new model when the provider releases one. Your prompts, parsers and eval scores were tuned on the old behaviour, so quality, format or cost can shift with no deploy on your side. A pinned dated snapshot gives reproducibility and a controlled upgrade: I test the new model on my eval suite, canary it, then change the pin.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A snapshot is a specific frozen model version with a dated id; an alias is a moving name that points to the newest snapshot. With an alias, an upgrade is an unannounced change to a core dependency, like a library that auto-updates in production. Snapshots also get deprecated on a published schedule, so pinning does not remove work: it moves the migration to a time you choose. Keep the model id in config (not scattered in code), record it in every trace, and keep an abstraction layer so a swap is one change. Also pin the judge model used in evals, or scores drift without any change in your system.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Pinning the model but not the prompt, tools or retrieval config.
  • Forgetting deprecation dates until the snapshot is retired.
  • Hard-coding the id in many files.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does pinning guarantee identical output? → No, sampling is still random; it guarantees the same weights/behaviour class.
  2. How do you upgrade? → Eval suite, review diffs, shadow, canary, rollback to the old pin.
  3. What if only an alias exists? → Log the resolved model id from the response and alert on change.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "pin for stability." Senior: treats upgrade as a release, tracks deprecation calendar, pins judge too, logs resolved id.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A silent alias update changed JSON formatting habits and broke a strict parser overnight.

questions.promptHtml: An LLM API call fails with 429 or 503 occasionally. How do you handle it, and what should you not retry?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline reliability judgement for any API-backed system.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I set a timeout on every call and retry only transient errors (429, 5xx, timeouts) with exponential backoff plus jitter, honoring the retry-after header, with a small attempt cap. I never retry 400-class errors like invalid request, because they will fail forever. Only one layer of the stack retries, otherwise retries multiply.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: 429 means rate limited, 5xx means server trouble. Exponential backoff doubles the wait each attempt (1s, 2s, 4s); jitter adds randomness so many clients do not retry at the same instant (a retry storm). With 3 layers each retrying 3 times, one failure becomes 27 calls, so centralise retries. Calls with side effects (a tool that charges money) need an idempotency key. Many SDKs already retry by default, so check before adding your own.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import random, time
from anthropic import Anthropic, RateLimitError, APIStatusError
client = Anthropic()

def call(msg, tries=4):
    for i in range(tries):
        try:
            return client.messages.create(model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=200,
                       messages=[{"role": "user", "content": msg}], timeout=20)
        except RateLimitError:
            pass
        except APIStatusError as e:
            if e.status_code < 500: raise   # 4xx: do not retry
        time.sleep(min(30, 2 ** i) * random.uniform(0.5, 1.5))
    raise RuntimeError("exhausted")
suspend fun <T> retrying(tries: Int = 4, block: suspend () -> T): T {
    repeat(tries - 1) { i ->
        try { return block() } catch (e: TransientException) {
            kotlinx.coroutines.delay((minOf(30_000L, 1000L shl i) * (0.5 + Math.random())).toLong())
        }
    }
    return block() // last attempt; TransientException = your mapping of 429/5xx/timeout
}
static <T> T retrying(java.util.concurrent.Callable<T> c, int tries) throws Exception {
    for (int i = 0; ; i++) {
        try { return c.call(); }
        catch (TransientException e) {           // your mapping of 429/5xx/timeout
            if (i == tries - 1) throw e;
            Thread.sleep((long) (Math.min(30_000, 1000L << i) * (0.5 + Math.random())));
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No jitter, so clients retry in lockstep.
  • Retrying 400s and burning quota.
  • Retries at gateway, SDK and app layers at once.
  • No overall deadline, so users wait a minute.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why honour retry-after? → The server tells you when capacity returns.
  2. What next after retries fail? → Fallback model, cached or simplified answer, queue.
  3. How do you retry a tool that writes data? → Idempotency key.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "retry with backoff." Senior: single retry layer, retry budgets, deadlines, idempotency, circuit breaker.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 429 burst triggered nested retries that tripled load and prolonged the outage.

questions.promptHtml: Explain shadow deployment, canary release and A/B test for an LLM change. When do you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Release hygiene: can you ship prompt/model changes safely?

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Shadow runs the new version on real traffic in parallel but hides its output, so I compare safely. Canary sends the new version to a small slice (1 to 5%) of real users with auto-rollback on guardrail breaches. A/B randomly splits users to measure which version is better on a pre-declared metric. Shadow checks it works, canary checks it is safe, A/B checks it is better.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Shadow costs double inference but has zero user risk; good for model upgrades. Canary exposes real users, so define rollback triggers first (error rate, latency, refusal rate, cost per request). A/B needs a primary metric, guardrail metrics, a sample size computed beforehand, and randomisation by user (not by request) so one user sees one variant. Feature flags and kill switches let you flip without redeploying.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import hashlib
def in_canary(user_id: str, pct: int) -> bool:
    return int(hashlib.sha256(user_id.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100 < pct  # stable per user
fun inCanary(userId: String, pct: Int): Boolean =
    java.math.BigInteger(1, java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
        .digest(userId.toByteArray())).mod(java.math.BigInteger.valueOf(100)).toInt() < pct
static boolean inCanary(String userId, int pct) throws Exception {
    byte[] h = java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(userId.getBytes());
    return new java.math.BigInteger(1, h).mod(java.math.BigInteger.valueOf(100)).intValue() < pct;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Random per request, so a user flips between variants.
  • Peeking at A/B results early and stopping on noise.
  • Judging by one metric and ignoring cost and safety.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why hash the user id? → Stable assignment and reproducibility.
  2. Which guardrails? → Latency, errors, cost, refusal, escalation, complaints.
  3. When skip A/B? → When a fast offline eval plus canary is enough evidence.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: defines the three terms. Senior: sequences them, defines rollback automation and guardrails.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A prompt tweak won on thumbs-up but doubled tokens; only the cost guardrail caught it.

questions.contextHtml: Your support bot uses model: "provider-chat-latest" (an alias). Nothing was deployed for 9 days. Thumbs-up rate fell from 82% to 71%, and the JSON parser error rate rose from 0.4% to 3.1%. Traffic is steady at 40k requests/day. The retrieval index was re-built 12 days ago. A teammate blames the retrieval team.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find the cause and stop it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back the last deploy" (there was none) or "tweak the prompt until it works", with no evidence and no versioning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do traces record the resolved model id? Did the drop start on a specific day? Is it uniform across features or concentrated? Any provider announcements?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a lenient parser/repair step and, if a previous snapshot is still available, pin to it for the worst feature.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) alias moved to a new model, (b) data drift in queries, (c) index rebuild 12 days ago, (d) library/tokenizer change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group trace metrics by resolved model id and by day: a step on one day aligned with an id change implicates (a). Run the golden set against old and new snapshot. Compare query-topic clusters week over week for (b). The index rebuilt 12 days ago predates the drop by 3 days, a red herring unless the metrics step at that date.
  5. Root cause: The alias moved; the new model formats JSON differently and answers more verbosely.
  6. Fix: Short term: pin the old snapshot. Long term: adapt prompt and parser, run the eval suite on the new model, then canary and migrate on schedule.
  7. Prevention: Pin snapshots, log resolved ids, alert on id change and on parser error rate, scheduled evals on a production sample.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite retrieval on a hunch. Pinning delays gains from the new model, so I schedule the migration.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The old snapshot is deprecated next month? → Plan the migration now with the eval suite and a canary.
  • Resolved id never changed? → Then look at data drift and the index.
  • Provider gives no old snapshot? → Fix prompt and parser, add a fallback provider.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team lost a week blaming retrieval before a per-model-id chart showed the step on the exact day an alias flipped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: guesses and edits prompts blindly.
  • Hire: segments metrics by model id and pins the snapshot.
  • Strong hire: also adds change alerts, evals on the new model and a migration plan.

questions.promptHtml: How would you wire LLM evals into a CI/CD pipeline without making it slow or expensive?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: LLM changes have no compiler; evals are your tests. Interviewers want a tiered, cost-aware design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I tier it. On every PR: fast deterministic checks (prompt lint, schema validation, parser unit tests) and a 20-50 case smoke eval. When a PR touches prompts, retrieval, models or tools: the golden set, compared with the baseline using confidence intervals, failing on regressions beyond a threshold. Nightly: the full suite, red-team and long-tail slices, and cost/latency benchmarks. Before release: shadow or canary. After release: sample production for auto-eval and feed failures back as new cases.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A golden set is a curated list of inputs with expected behaviour or grading criteria. An LLM-as-judge is a model that scores answers against a rubric; pin it and calibrate it against human labels. Outputs are random, so run repeats and compare score distributions, not single runs; otherwise tests flake. Control cost by caching cases whose inputs and versions did not change, sampling on PRs, and using a cheaper model for the smoke tier. The PR report should show score deltas by slice and the new failures with examples. Safety-critical changes need human sign-off.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One accuracy number with no slices.
  • Unpinned judge model.
  • Running the full suite on every commit.
  • Fixed thresholds ignoring run-to-run noise.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How avoid flakes? → Repeats, confidence intervals, quarantine flaky cases.
  2. Where do new cases come from? → Production failures.
  3. How do you judge the judge? → Agreement with human labels, periodic recalibration.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "run a test set." Senior: tiers, stats, cost control, judge calibration, feedback into the dataset.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A prompt "improvement" passed the overall score but broke a 4% slice of refund questions; slice reporting caught it.

questions.contextHtml: The monthly LLM bill jumped from $18k to $31k with traffic up only 6%. Dashboards show total tokens only. Average latency is unchanged. Two features, "summarize" and "agent assistant", share one API key. A new tenant onboarded last week.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find where the cost came from, and what do you put in place?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to a cheaper model" without locating the source.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which model/ids? Input vs output token split? Cache hit rate change? Release in that window?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add per-tenant rate and token budgets, plus a spend alert.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one tenant sending huge documents, (b) agent loop with extra turns, (c) prompt grew after a change (bigger context or few-shots), (d) cache hit rate dropped after a prompt-prefix edit, (e) retries.
  4. How I'd verify each: Need traces: cost grouped by tenant, feature, model and prompt version. Compare input tokens per request across weeks; check cache hit rate; check average turns per agent session and retry counts. Latency being flat is a red herring: cost scales with tokens, not time.
  5. Root cause (example): The new tenant's 60k-token documents plus an agent loop averaging 9 turns instead of 4.
  6. Fix: Cap turns and input size, truncate or summarise long inputs, route easy cases to a smaller model, restore a stable prompt prefix for caching.
  7. Prevention: Tag every call with tenant/feature, budgets, anomaly alerts, cost per request in the PR eval report.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not downgrade the model globally; it may cut quality for all tenants to fix one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Shared key prevents attribution? → Use per-feature keys and tag requests in your own gateway.
  • Quality drops with the smaller model? → Route only classified-easy requests.
  • Tenant refuses limits? → Offer a higher tier or a batch mode.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single unbounded loop bug in one tenant burnt a month's budget in two days before spend alerts existed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps model blindly.
  • Hire: attributes cost by tenant/feature and finds the driver.
  • Strong hire: also sets budgets, alerts and cost gates in CI.

questions.promptHtml: What should be versioned in an LLM application beyond the code, and how would you tie versions to each deployment and request?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reproducibility and rollback depend on knowing the full configuration.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Prompts, model snapshot, sampling parameters, tool schemas, retrieval config (chunking, embedding model, index version, reranker), guardrail policies, eval datasets and judges, and fine-tuned weights. I keep them in Git or a prompt registry with immutable versions and labels like prod, and build a manifest listing every version, attached to the deployment and to each trace. Then I can explain, reproduce and roll back precisely.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A manifest is one small file saying "this release = prompt v14 + model snapshot X + index v7 + tools v3". Immutability matters: you never edit v14, you publish v15 and move the prod label. Indexes use aliases and blue/green re-indexing so rollback is a pointer change. Schema changes follow semantic versioning and need coordinated prompt, parser and consumer updates.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import json, hashlib
manifest = {"prompt": "support@v14", "model": "claude-sonnet-5-5", "index": "kb@v7",
            "tools": "tools@v3", "guardrails": "policy@v2"}
manifest["id"] = hashlib.sha1(json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
# attach manifest["id"] to every trace so a bad answer maps to an exact configuration
val manifest = mapOf("prompt" to "support@v14", "model" to "claude-sonnet-5-5",
                     "index" to "kb@v7", "tools" to "tools@v3")
val manifestId = manifest.toSortedMap().toString().hashCode().toString(16) // use a real hash in production
Map<String, String> manifest = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(
    "prompt", "support@v14", "model", "claude-sonnet-5-5", "index", "kb@v7", "tools", "tools@v3"));
String manifestId = Integer.toHexString(manifest.toString().hashCode()); // use SHA-256 in production

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Versioning prompts but not retrieval or tool schemas.
  • Editing a prompt version in place.
  • Rolling back code while the index already moved.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why labels? → Move prod without changing content.
  2. Reproduce an old answer? → Rebuild from the manifest; seeds help but outputs may still vary.
  3. Schema change safety? → Backward-compatible versions and coordinated release.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "prompts in Git." Senior: full manifest, immutable versions, index aliases, per-trace stamping.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rollback restored the old prompt but the new index stayed, giving broken citations until the manifest exposed the mismatch.

questions.contextHtml: At 14:02 the provider returns 529 overloaded for 4 minutes. Your service normally makes 120 LLM calls/s. During the incident you observe 900 calls/s outbound, the 429 rate climbs, and when the provider recovers at 14:06 your errors continue until 14:20. The gateway, the SDK (default 2 retries) and your app (3 retries) all retry with fixed 1s delay.
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the retry count" or "provider's fault."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many layers retry? Is there jitter? Is there a deadline? Is there a circuit breaker?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce traffic with load shedding, disable retries in two layers, enable a fallback response.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stacked retries amplify load (up to 3 x 3 x 2 attempts per request), (b) no jitter synchronises waves, (c) no breaker keeps hammering, (d) queue backlog delays recovery.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare outbound calls per inbound request in metrics; check retry headers/logs per layer; plot request rate at 1s periodicity.
  5. Root cause: A retry storm: amplification of load of roughly 7x kept the provider and our rate limit saturated after the real fault ended.
  6. Fix: One retry layer, exponential backoff with jitter, honour retry-after, a retry budget (for example retries at most 10% of traffic), a circuit breaker, a fallback model or cached answer, and an end-to-end deadline.
  7. Prevention: Failure-injection drill, alerts on outbound/inbound ratio.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not remove retries entirely: transient errors are real. Breakers can reject healthy traffic if tuned too tight.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fallback provider also has limits? → Bulkhead pools and shed low-priority traffic.
  • Calls have side effects? → Idempotency keys.
  • Streaming dropped mid-answer? → Retry only if nothing was shown, or resume with context.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 4-minute provider blip became a 18-minute outage of our own making because three layers retried in lockstep.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the provider.
  • Hire: identifies retry amplification and fixes with backoff and jitter.
  • Strong hire: adds budgets, breaker, fallback and drills.

questions.promptHtml: What feedback signals can you collect from an LLM product, and what biases should you watch for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Improvement depends on turning usage into signal while knowing its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Explicit: thumbs, ratings, reports, human corrections. Implicit: regenerate clicks, copy, edits to the output, abandonment, rephrased follow-ups, escalation to a human, task completion events. Plus expert review of sampled transcripts and automated judges on sampled traffic. Biases: only extremes bother to click thumbs, implicit signals are ambiguous, users can game it, and reusing data needs consent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The loop: collect, cluster failures, root-cause (retrieval, prompt, tool, model or data), fix, add as regression cases, evaluate, release, measure. Thumbs-down rate of 3% from 1% of users says little about the silent 96%; implicit signals have higher coverage but need interpretation (a regenerate may mean curiosity). Treat edits and corrections as the highest-value labels. Training on the model's own outputs risks reinforcing its errors, so keep human or verified labels in the loop.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating thumbs-up rate as true quality.
  • Using user data for training without consent and review.
  • No deduplication of curated corrections.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Best implicit signal? → Task completion or edit distance on accepted output.
  2. How do you make feedback actionable? → Cluster by topic and root cause.
  3. Can you fine-tune on feedback? → Yes with consent, privacy review and dedup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "add thumbs buttons." Senior: signal taxonomy, bias awareness, closed loop into regression sets.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Thumbs-up stayed flat while escalations rose 20%; only the implicit signal revealed a regression.

questions.contextHtml: Your PR eval runs 300 cases with an LLM judge and fails the build if the score drops 1 point. The same commit scores 84.2, 82.9 and 85.1 on three re-runs. Developers have started re-running until green. Eval costs $6 per run, and the judge model is the unpinned default.
questions.promptHtml: Fix the gate so it is trustworthy.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Loosen the threshold to 5 points", which hides real regressions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Temperature of the model under test and the judge? Judge pinned? Are failures concentrated in some cases?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin the judge and set temperature to a low value for grading; stop manual re-runs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) judge variance, (b) sampling noise of the system under test, (c) small-sample noise (300 cases, a 1-point spread is within the standard error), (d) flaky ambiguous cases.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the same commit 10 times and compute the standard deviation; per-case pass-rate across runs identifies flaky cases; judge-vs-human agreement on a labelled subset.
  5. Root cause: Noise of about +/-1.2 points exceeded the 1-point threshold.
  6. Fix: Pin the judge, use paired comparison against the baseline on identical cases, run 3 repeats, use a confidence interval and fail only when the interval excludes zero, quarantine flaky cases, rewrite ambiguous rubrics.
  7. Prevention: Store scores over time, track variance, recalibrate the judge on a schedule.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not run 20 repeats everywhere (cost: 20 x $6 = $120 per PR); apply it only to PRs that touch prompts or models.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Budget capped? → Cache unchanged cases and sample.
  • Real regression only in a slice? → Report per slice with its own interval.
  • Judge changes provider? → Recalibrate against human labels first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A gate that was re-run until green ended up blocking nothing; replacing it with paired comparisons restored trust within a sprint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: widens the threshold.
  • Hire: pins the judge and uses repeats and intervals.
  • Strong hire: paired design, flaky quarantine, cost-aware tiers.

questions.promptHtml: What kinds of drift affect a deployed LLM application, and how do you detect and manage each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Production systems degrade without code changes; seniors anticipate it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Model drift (provider updates or unpinned aliases), data drift (new topics, products, languages), concept drift (policies change, for example a new refund rule), infrastructure drift (library, tokenizer or API changes), adversary drift (new jailbreaks) and embedding or index drift (stale or mixed vectors). I pin versions, run scheduled evals on production samples, monitor query-topic distributions and retrieval health, and keep a deprecation calendar.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Detect: cluster queries weekly and compare distributions; track retrieval hit rate and average top score; track judge scores on sampled traffic; alert on shifts. Manage: refresh the golden set with recent traffic, re-index on a schedule, review prompts after policy changes, refresh the red-team suite. Mixed embeddings (some documents embedded with an old model) quietly break similarity search, so version the embedding model with the index.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Evaluating only on the launch-day dataset.
  • Updating the corpus without re-checking answers that cite it.
  • Ignoring deprecation dates.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cheapest drift detector? → Weekly topic-cluster and score trend on sampled traffic.
  2. Concept drift example? → The refund window changes from 30 to 14 days; old docs linger.
  3. How do you rehearse deprecation? → Migration drills against the eval suite.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "monitor accuracy." Senior: names the six drift sources with a detector and an owner for each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Old and new policy documents coexisted in the index and the bot quoted whichever ranked higher.

questions.contextHtml: You A/B test a new prompt on 2,000 users per arm over 3 days. Thumbs-up: 78.0% vs 79.4% (p = 0.31). Average cost per request rose 22%, p95 latency rose from 3.1s to 3.9s. The product manager says "it's better, ship it."
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Ships it because the number is higher, or declares it a failure without reasoning about power.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What was the pre-declared primary metric and minimum detectable effect? Do thumbs reach most users? Any novelty effect over 3 days? Segment differences?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not ship; keep the control while collecting more data.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no real quality difference, (b) underpowered: detecting 1.4 points at about 78% needs several thousand users per arm, (c) segment effects hidden in the average, (d) weekday-only effects.
  4. How I'd verify each: Power calculation, breakdown by segment, a longer run covering a full week, an additional metric such as task completion.
  5. Root cause of the confusion: The test was underpowered and decided on one weak signal while guardrails got worse.
  6. Fix: Recommend no ship: the quality gain is not significant, and cost +22% and latency +0.8s are real costs. Optionally rerun with a larger sample or optimise the prompt for tokens.
  7. Prevention: Pre-register the metric, sample size and guardrails before the test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not peek and stop early, and not cherry-pick a favourable segment after the fact.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Quality improved for new users only? → Plan a segment-specific rollout and confirm with a follow-up test.
  • Cost is acceptable? → Then the decision depends on the latency budget.
  • Need results sooner? → Use a larger traffic share rather than shorter duration.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "obviously better" prompt shipped on a 1-point lift and added six figures to annual spend with no measurable satisfaction gain.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: ships on the point estimate.
  • Hire: notes non-significance and guardrail regressions.
  • Strong hire: power analysis, segments and a pre-registered plan.

questions.promptHtml: Your traces contain full prompts and responses that include customer data. How do you keep observability without becoming a privacy liability?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Observability data is often the largest uncontrolled copy of sensitive data.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I treat traces as sensitive data stores. I redact PII and secrets before storage, keep metadata (versions, tokens, latency, ids) always and full payloads only on a sample or on errors, restrict access by role, set retention, and support deletion by user id. For regulated tenants, I allow metadata-only tracing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PII means personally identifiable information. Redaction can use pattern matchers (emails, card numbers) plus an NER (named entity recognition) model; it is imperfect, so also encrypt at rest and limit access. Hashing user ids allows joining without exposing identity. Tiered retention: metadata for a year, payloads for 7 to 30 days. Provide deletion hooks for data-subject requests. Debug access should be logged and time-limited. The trade-off: less payload means harder debugging, so use sampling plus on-demand capture when a user opts in during a support case.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Redacting only the input and logging the response, which echoes PII.
  • Sending raw traces to a third-party SaaS without review.
  • No retention or deletion path.
  • Tool outputs and retrieved chunks forgotten in the redaction.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How judge quality without payloads? → Run evaluators in-process and store only scores.
  2. Deletion request? → Index traces by hashed user id and purge.
  3. Self-host or SaaS? → Depends on data residency and contract; verify with legal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "mask emails." Senior: tiered data, retention, access control, deletion path, and in-process evaluation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A debug dashboard exposed support chats to all engineers until access controls and retention were added.

questions.contextHtml: Your provider will retire the pinned snapshot in 60 days. The newer model is 30% cheaper per token but wordier. You serve 2M requests/day across 5 features. A smoke test of the new model passes, but on your 1,200-case golden set it scores 91.2 vs 92.0 overall, and 14 points lower on the extraction feature (strict JSON). Legal requires no disclosure regressions.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out the migration.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Swap the id and watch dashboards."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which features are the highest risk? Are there contractual quality commitments? Can we run two models in parallel? Rollback allowed until the retirement date?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed yet; block the deadline risk by scheduling.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the format regression is fixable via prompt or structured output, (b) verbosity raises output cost, eroding the 30% saving, (c) refusal and safety behaviours differ.
  4. How I'd verify each: Diff failure cases by feature; compute cost per request with real output lengths (cost = tokens x price, check output share); run the safety/red-team suite; then shadow on live traffic.
  5. Root cause of the extraction gap: the new model wraps JSON in prose; the prompt assumed bare output.
  6. Fix: Adapt prompts per feature, use structured outputs/schema enforcement, re-run evals, shadow 100% for a week, canary 1%, 5%, 25%, 100% per feature, keeping the old snapshot as rollback until the final week.
  7. Prevention: Deprecation calendar, a standing eval suite, an abstraction layer for model ids.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not migrate all features at once; if extraction cannot be fixed in time, use the new model only for the features that pass and push the provider for an extension.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retirement moved to 30 days? → Prioritise the highest-volume passing features first.
  • Judge disagrees with humans on the new style? → Recalibrate with human labels.
  • Costs rise despite lower price? → Cap max tokens and instruct brevity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "cheaper" model cost more in practice after verbosity; only per-feature cost tracking showed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps and hopes.
  • Hire: evals, shadow, canary, rollback.
  • Strong hire: per-feature gating, cost analysis with real output lengths, and a deadline plan.

questions.promptHtml: Design the failure-handling strategy for an LLM-backed feature that must stay available when the primary provider degrades.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks system design thinking beyond "retry".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Layered: timeouts and a deadline, one retry layer, a circuit breaker per dependency, then fallbacks in order of preference: secondary model or provider, cached or simplified answer, non-AI path, queue for later. Under load, degrade optional features (reranking, long memory) and shed low-priority traffic. Bulkhead pools isolate features and tenants. SLOs with error budgets decide how much risk to take on releases.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing dependency for a cool-down period, then probes with a few calls (half-open). Bulkheads give each feature its own concurrency pool, so one runaway feature cannot starve the rest. Fallback models need their own evals and prompts; a different provider means different formats and safety behaviour. Make fallbacks visible in traces (a fallback_used flag) and in alerts. Test with chaos drills: block the primary in staging and check the behaviour and the quality of the degraded answer.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A fallback prompt never tested, so it produces garbage in the incident.
  • The breaker threshold too sensitive, so it flaps.
  • A fallback provider with the same single point of failure (same cloud region).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the user see in degradation? → A clear simpler answer, not an error.
  2. How decide fallback order? → Quality, cost, latency, data residency.
  3. SLO example? → 99.5% of requests succeed within 8s; error budget guides risk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "retry and a backup model." Senior: breaker, bulkhead, degraded modes, tested fallbacks, SLO-driven governance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fallback to a smaller model passed health checks but answered in the wrong format, so downstream parsers failed until the fallback was evaluated like a primary.

questions.subtopic: Rollback that does not roll back
questions.contextHtml: A release changed the prompt (v14 to v15), the answer schema (adding a citations array, v3 to v4) and re-indexed the knowledge base with a new embedding model (index v7 to v8). Error rate hit 9% so you rolled back the code and prompt. Errors dropped only to 6%, and citations now point to the wrong passages. Traces record only the prompt version.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, how do you recover, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back again" without knowing what to roll back.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the old index still available? Did consumers already adopt schema v4? Which components were deployed together?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Point the index alias back to v7 (if retained) and serve schema v3; if the old index was deleted, disable citations via a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) index and embedding model mismatch with the query-side embedder, (b) consumers expecting v4, (c) parser version mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check embedding model ids on both query and index side, run a retrieval probe with known query-document pairs, inspect schema validation errors.
  5. Root cause: Three coupled changes shipped as one release while only one was versioned in traces; rollback covered one third.
  6. Fix: Restore a consistent manifest: prompt v14, schema v3, index v7, embedder matching the index.
  7. Prevention: A manifest per release and per trace, immutable indexes with aliases (blue/green), keep the old index until stability, ship coupled changes behind flags, and rehearse rollback.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Keeping two indexes doubles storage temporarily; splitting the release into three costs time but makes each reversible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The old index was deleted? → Rebuild from the source with the old embedder; meanwhile degrade gracefully.
  • Consumers on v4 already? → Support both with backward-compatible fields.
  • How to detect embedder mismatch early? → Store the embedder id in index metadata and assert on query.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "rollback" restored half the system, and an hour was lost until someone listed every changed artifact.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: re-deploys the old code only.
  • Hire: identifies all coupled artifacts and restores consistency.
  • Strong hire: manifest, immutable index aliases and rollback drills.

questions.contextHtml: Leadership wants a "data flywheel": every night, fine-tune the model on conversations that got a thumbs-up (about 6,000 per day, only 1.5% of users vote). After three weeks, thumbs-up rose from 80% to 88%, but the eval golden set fell from 90 to 85, answers are shorter and more flattering, and legal asks whether users consented.
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate the design and propose a safer one.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Celebrates the thumbs-up rise.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Consent text and terms? Does thumbs correlate with task success? Are outputs included from earlier fine-tuned versions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause nightly training and roll back to the last checkpoint that scored 90.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the model optimises for approval (flattery, shortness), (b) selection bias: 1.5% of users vote, mostly on easy cases, (c) self-training on its own outputs reinforces errors, (d) duplicates and noise in labels.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare golden-set slices, answer length and sycophancy probes before and after, examine voter vs non-voter demographics, check duplicate rates and overlap with the eval set (leakage).
  5. Root cause: Training on a biased, self-generated, unverified signal without a held-out gate.
  6. Fix: Curate: use human corrections, expert-reviewed samples and verified outcomes rather than raw thumbs; dedupe; get consent and run a privacy review; gate each candidate on the golden set and red-team suite; release through canary.
  7. Prevention: Hold-out evals never trained on, periodic fresh human audits, rate limits on training cadence.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not fine-tune daily; weekly curated batches are slower but safer. Consider prompt or retrieval fixes first since they are cheaper and reversible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Little data of the right kind? → Few-shot examples from curated corrections.
  • Need faster iteration? → Fix retrieval and prompts, fine-tune rarely.
  • Users asked deletion? → Track provenance to remove their data from future training sets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A model trained on approval signals learned to agree with users, and satisfaction rose while accuracy fell.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: trusts thumbs-up.
  • Hire: spots bias, consent and the need for hold-out evals.
  • Strong hire: curated pipeline, gates, canary and cheaper alternatives.

questions.contextHtml: You sample 1% of production (about 5,000 traces/day) for a judge model that scores groundedness. The score declined smoothly from 0.91 to 0.84 over six weeks while users' thumbs-up stayed flat and no deploys changed prompts. The judge model is an unpinned alias. Human spot checks of 100 traces show 88% of answers acceptable, consistent with before.
questions.promptHtml: Is quality dropping? How do you decide?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts to rewrite prompts to raise the judge score.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the judge's model id logged? Did the traffic mix change? Same rubric text?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No user-facing change; freeze the alert threshold and investigate, since flat thumbs and human checks suggest no regression.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) judge drift (an alias update changed its strictness), (b) traffic mix shifted to harder questions, (c) a real slow decline in retrieval quality, (d) corpus changes lowering grounding.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-score a frozen set of 300 old traces with today's judge: if scores fall, the judge moved. Break the score down by topic. Compare retrieval top scores over time. Measure judge-human agreement on the 100 labelled traces.
  5. Root cause (likely): The judge alias changed, giving lower scores for the same answers.
  6. Fix: Pin the judge, recalibrate against human labels, reset the baseline with a documented change, keep an anchor set scored every run.
  7. Prevention: Anchor set of frozen traces for judge drift, human spot checks monthly, log the judge id in every score.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not trust a single metric; judges are models too and need monitoring.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Anchor scores also fell for answers? → Then suspect the data or the system, not the judge.
  • Human checks are expensive? → Sample smaller but stratified.
  • Two judges disagree? → Use pairwise comparison and calibrate on labels.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dashboard score fell 7 points after a silent judge update, and a team spent a sprint "fixing" a model that was fine.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: optimises the score.
  • Hire: suspects the judge and re-scores old data.
  • Strong hire: anchor sets, pinned judge and human calibration.

questions.contextHtml: The primary provider's region fails for 47 minutes. Your fallback to a second provider activates, but its p95 latency is 11s (against an 8s timeout), so 38% of fallback requests time out. The fallback prompt was last tested six months ago, and it returned a different JSON key (answer_text) in 12% of cases, breaking parsing. The error budget for the month (0.5% = about 216 minutes of full outage-equivalent) was consumed 22%.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: what failed, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "We had a fallback, so it worked", ignoring that it was untested.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the fallback run in staging drills? Were its latency and format evaluated? Was traffic shed by priority?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (what we should have done) shed low-priority traffic, raise the fallback timeout with a deadline-aware budget, serve a cached or simplified answer for the top intents.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) untested fallback prompt and schema, (b) timeouts tuned for the primary, (c) fallback capacity not reserved, (d) no degraded mode.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay recorded traffic against the fallback in staging, compare schema validity and latency percentiles, and review the traces tagged fallback_used.
  5. Root cause: The fallback path was treated as a configuration option rather than a product that needs evals, load tests and drills.
  6. Fix: Evaluate the fallback on the golden set, normalise outputs with a schema validator and key mapping, set per-provider timeouts, reserve capacity, add a degraded mode (cached answers, disable reranking), and monthly failover drills.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on the fallback share, scheduled chaos drills, SLOs per provider, a runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A hot standby costs money and prompt maintenance; weigh against the revenue at risk. Not run active-active with no quality parity checks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Both providers degrade? → Non-AI path and queue for later.
  • How much of the budget should drills use? → Small and planned, in low traffic.
  • Is the 22% budget burn acceptable? → Compare to what the drill-based design would have cost (likely under 5%).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A standby model that had never taken live traffic failed in new ways on the first day it was needed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the provider.
  • Hire: tests fallbacks, adjusts timeouts and schemas.
  • Strong hire: drills, degraded modes, error-budget policy and capacity planning.
